blocks.h: Why does the sign trick work?
p: Every value is in 1…n, so the array itself can act as a hash set whose keys are the indexes. Each value appears once or twice, so a slot is marked at most twice: the second marking attempt finds it already negative and reports a duplicate. This gives O(1) extra space; the trade-off is that the input array is modified (it ends up with negative entries).

442.takeaway: Use the array as its own visited set: negate nums[|x|−1] on first sight, and a second visit means x is a duplicate.

p: `[4,3,2,7,8,2,3,1]` after marking: `[-4, -3, -2, -7, 8, 2, -3, -1]`. Positions 4 and 5 (0-based) are still positive, so the missing numbers are [5, 6].

blocks.h: Why `-abs(nums[i])` here but plain negation in problem 442?
p: Here duplicates are expected and harmless: marking an already-negative slot must keep it negative. With `-nums[i]` the second mark of a duplicate value (2 and 3 both appear twice) would flip the slot back to positive and wrongly report it as missing.

448.takeaway: Negate nums[|x|−1] for every x; the indexes that stay positive are the missing values.

blocks.h: A case with no valid cycle: `[-1,2]`
p: Returns False. Start 0 moves backward 0→1 (index −1 mod 2 = 1); there nums[1] = 2 is forward, so the direction changes and the walk ends; both visited indexes are zeroed.

Without it, every start could re-walk long chains: O(n²). A walk that fails can never become part of a valid cycle (the direction rule or a self-loop broke it), so its indexes can be disabled for all later starts. The cost is that the input is modified.

bullets: Time: O(n) — each index is walked in at most one failed path.
Space: O(n) for `seen` in this version (the classic fast/slow pointer version uses O(1)).

457.takeaway: Follow same-direction jumps from each start; a repeat means a cycle, and failed paths are zeroed so work stays linear.

blocks.h: Why BFS over stops, not cells?
p: The ball can't change direction mid-roll, so the only decisions are made at stopping squares. Treating each full roll as one edge keeps the graph small. A square the ball only passes through is not a node, which is why the destination check is done on popped stops.

bullets: Time: O(m·n·(m+n)): at most m·n stops, each rolling up to m or n cells in four directions.

490.takeaway: BFS on stopping points: each push rolls the ball to a wall; only squares where it stops become graph nodes.

blocks.h: Why greedy by profit among affordable projects?
p: Capital only grows, so a project that is affordable now stays affordable later. Taking the largest profit now never prevents any future option and gives the most capital for unlocking the next projects. The heap holds all currently affordable profits so the best one is available in O(log n).

bullets: Time: O(n log n): sorting plus each project pushed and popped at most once.

502.takeaway: Greedy with a max-heap: unlock every project you can afford, take the most profitable, repeat up to k times.

When to reach for it

Best known distance to each stopping square
Used to relax and to skip stale heap entries
A square can be pushed several times; only the freshest matters

p: Same maze as the previous problem (`00100 / 00000 / 00010 / 11011 / 00000`), start (0,4), destination (4,4). Result: 12.

blocks.h: Why Dijkstra and not BFS (Breadth-First Search)?
p: BFS assumes every move costs the same. Here a push can roll 1 cell or 7, so the move with the fewest pushes isn't necessarily the shortest. Dijkstra pops the stop with the smallest total distance, so the first time the destination is popped, its distance is optimal.

bullets: Time: O(m·n·log(m·n)) heap operations (each stop is expanded a few times, plus the rolling cost of up to m+n cells per expansion).

505.takeaway: Dijkstra over stopping points: edge weight is the rolled distance, popped in order of smallest total distance.

p: If prefix[j] and prefix[i] leave the same remainder when divided by k, their difference, the sum of nums[j+1..i], is divisible by k. The code assumes k ≥ 1 (with k = 0 the `%` would raise `ZeroDivisionError`), which the problem guarantees.

523.takeaway: Prefix sums modulo k with a first-seen map: equal remainders at least two apart mean a multiple-of-k subarray.

blocks.h: Why is a `seen` set enough and no recursion order matters?
p: A province is a connected component. Once a DFS from city i has marked every city reachable from i, none of them can start another count. So the number of times the outer loop finds an unvisited city equals the number of components.

bullets: Time: O(n²): every row of the matrix is scanned once.

547.takeaway: Count connected components: loop over cities and start a DFS (Depth-First Search) from each one that is not yet visited.
